title: Managed hosting
summary: Map a managed platform’s process, assigned port, and external configuration to the Boot application.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Deploy Spring Boot App on Heroku: Easy Guide for Beginners

richText: The application process on managed hosting
A managed host starts the Boot JAR as a Java process. The JAR still starts its embedded server.
The platform’s Java version must support the compiled application.
The platform may build the project from source or accept an artifact. Its start command must point to the generated executable JAR.
Some platforms use a buildpack to select a runtime and prepare the start process. The host’s Java support determines the available runtime.
The assigned port
A platform may assign its HTTP port through an environment variable such as
PORT
c
Boot’s server property is
server.port
c
. A platform-specific variable must be mapped to that property unless the platform does it for the application.
A production profile can contain this mapping. Other external settings work as described in the configuration lessons.

example.title: Start the executable JAR with Heroku’s assigned port
description: Java `17` and Maven are required. The files form a separate project rooted at `pom.xml`.
This example uses Heroku’s classic process model. The platform supplies `PORT` and a Java `17` runtime.
`mvn clean package` creates `target/demo.jar`. `Procfile` supplies the platform start command.
explanation: `web` identifies the public web process in this platform’s process model.
The platform expands `$PORT` before Java starts.
`-Dserver.port` is a JVM system property, so it appears before `-jar`.
Boot reads this property and starts its embedded server on that assigned port.
The command describes the start process. It does not create databases or publish a working release by itself.

richText: External connections and storage
The platform’s secret system supplies database credentials and other sensitive configuration.
A correct database URI does not grant network access. The database must also permit connections from the deployed application.
Some application filesystems are temporary. A persistent database stores records outside the application process.
Uploaded files need persistent storage too. They are not made durable by including a JAR in the deployment.
Release behavior
Startup logs show whether the context and embedded server started. A public request checks whether the platform routes to them.
A health route can use the Actuator support explained earlier. A healthy route alone does not check every business operation.
A controlled authenticated request and data operation check the application’s actual configured dependencies.
The platform can stop and restart processes. Its stop timeout must allow Boot’s graceful shutdown to finish.
A previous JAR can restore previous application code. It does not undo a database migration or recover deleted records.
